text.p: NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank, said on Wednesday that the review if its operations being undertaken by acting chief executive Derek Wanless is not yet complete.
A spokeswoman for the investment bank said it regarded a report in Wednesday's Financial Times newspaper as "pure speculation" and declined to comment further.
The FT said the review would propose moving NatWest Markets' treasury operations, including foreign exchange and money market dealing, back into the main UK bank.
Wanless, who is also chief executive of the whole banking group was said by the FT to be in favour of the changes which could also include taking corporate lending away from NatWest Markets.

Like other banks, NatWest has scaled down its large corporate lending involvement due to the tiny margins on such business but analysts said the bank would have to weigh the effect of its actions on its client relationships.
But many analysts think the link between lending to large corporates and getting access to higher margin corporate advisory and finance business can be exaggerated.
They say other banks like Schroders and Goldman Sachs do well on the high margin side without getting involved in lending.

Analysts say the proposals, if carried out, would be largely cosmetic in the near term. They would free no capital, anyway NatWest has no capital shortage, and would just transfer profit streams from one business to the other.
But in the longer term it could be a useful move.

"It could be seen as cosmetic in the near-term but, in the sense that it increases their options for what to do with the business in the future, that's real," said John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers.

Analysts say the most difficult part of the proposal to realise would be the removal of the treasury operations. These are used both by the commercial bank and the investment bank, so the creation of a separate unit could be a possibility.
Wanless is consulting the global heads of the investment bank's divisions and is expected to make his recommendations to the NatWest Group board in the next few weeks.
The bank is expected to make at least a progress report when it publishes its first half results on August 5.

The review was announced in the wake of a 90 million pounds ($1519 million) loss in derivatives trading which led to the departure of chief executive Martin Owen and the resignation of other senior managers.
Wanless is said to have been under pressure from institutional investors to come up with a plan which will guarantee better returns for shareholders.
But some analysts say that tinkering with the structure of NatWest Markets will not be enough.
"Short of closing the whole thing down, I can't see much that is going to change the view of some investors," said one analyst.
